###### (1) Set up your working environment

Before running this code, make sure you are in the correct working directory with getwd() and setwd(). Otherwise you’ll have trouble tracking the data down!

Run this notebook in the CARC OnDemand RStudio session used for Materials Download Part 2. That assignment stored TCGA files in `~/490_cluster/analysis_data`. This notebook reads the previously downloaded BCR Biotab patient table directly and saves a CSV there for later runs; it does not contact the GDC server.

Set your working directory below:

```{r setup}
analysis_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "490_cluster", "analysis_data")
if (!dir.exists(analysis_dir)) {
  stop("Cannot find ", analysis_dir,
       ". Open CARC RStudio and locate the analysis_data folder from Materials Download Part 2.")
}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(analysis_dir))
as_num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(x)))
age_text <- function(x) {
  if (!length(x) || !is.finite(x[1])) "not available" else sprintf("%.1f years", x[1])
}

# Check all prerequisites before processing the worksheet.
required_packages <- c("survival", "survminer", "ggplot2")
missing_packages <- required_packages[!vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace,
                                               logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages)) {
  stop("In the CARC RStudio Console, run install.packages(c(",
       paste(sprintf('"%s"', missing_packages), collapse = ", "),
       ")), restart R, then Knit again.")
}
clinical_csv <- file.path(analysis_dir, "brca_clinical_data.csv")
if (!file.exists(clinical_csv)) {
  search_roots <- unique(c(file.path(analysis_dir, "GDCdata"),
                           file.path(dirname(analysis_dir), "GDCdata"),
                           file.path(path.expand("~"), "GDCdata"),
                           analysis_dir, dirname(analysis_dir)))
  search_roots <- search_roots[dir.exists(search_roots)]
  patient_files <- character()
  for (root in search_roots) {
    candidate_files <- list.files(root, pattern = "clinical_patient_brca[.]txt$",
                                  recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
    patient_files <- candidate_files[
      basename(candidate_files) == "nationwidechildrens.org_clinical_patient_brca.txt"]
    if (length(patient_files)) break
  }
  if (length(patient_files) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one previously downloaded BCR Biotab patient table ",
         "(nationwidechildrens.org_clinical_patient_brca.txt) under ",
         analysis_dir, " or its parent folders; found ", length(patient_files),
         ". Check the earlier CARC clinical download.")
  }
}
```

The personal repository’s `.gitignore` was checked: it already includes the following TCGA exclusions. 

      "### TCGA Data
      GDCdata
      MANIFEST*
      htseq_h5*
      analysis_data"

The .gitignore file lets Github know which files to NOT push. The loaded files from TCGA are quite large, so we don't want to push them to GitHub. It's also typically best to avoid putting raw data on GitHub.


###### (1) Example data frames

Going back to variables and object types, data frames are objects that store two-dimensional representations of data, often with row and column names. Data frames are the bread and butter of data analysis in R!

Let's explore the built in mtcars data frame before we get to using the TCGA datafram to learn about this crucial data type.

First, load in the data frame by running the following line of code. "mtcars" will then show up under "Data" in your environment panel.

```{r exercise-1-1}
data(mtcars)
```

The easiest way to view a data frame is to simply click on it in your environment tab! This will open up the matrix in a new tab. You can then explore the data visually.

However, this is not always helpful, especially when looking at larger or more complex data frames. We can use head() and str() to give us a better view in the console itself.

```{r exercise-1-2}
head(mtcars) # just like in the terminal, you can use head to view the first few rows of a data frame
```

Here we can see the first 6 rows of the mtcars data frame. We can see the row names (Mazda RX4, Mazda RX4 Wag, etc.), the column names (mpg, cyl, disp, etc.), and the data types associated with each column (dbl: double-precision floating point number).

```{r exercise-1-3}
str(mtcars) # str stands for structure
```

Running str() will give us info about the structure of the data frame. We can see the data type (data.frame), the number of rows (obs.) and columns (variables), the general data type of each column (num), and a preview of the data in each column.

The `$` operator accesses a named column in a data frame.
For example, `df_name$column_name` extracts one column.

Use this syntax to view the mpg column of the mtcars data frame.

```{r exercise-1-4}
mtcars$mpg
```

What if we want to view a column, but don't know it's exact name? We can get all column names (or all row names) by using the functions colnames() and rownames(). Call those below, then view the carburetor column using dollar sign notation.

```{r exercise-1-5}
colnames(mtcars)
rownames(mtcars)
mtcars$carb
```

We can also view particular subsets of the data frame by using the df[row, column] notation.

```{r exercise-1-6}
mtcars[2, 4] # access the value from the second row, fourth column (this is the horsepower of a Mazda RX4 Wag)

mtcars[1,  ] # access all values in the first row (all info on the Mazda RX4)

mtcars[ , 1] # access all values in the first column (mpg info for all cars)

mtcars[1:5, c(1, 4, 6)] # rows one through five and columns 1, 4, and 6

mtcars[-(3:30), ] # access everything EXCEPT rows 3 through 30

mtcars[ , c(-(1:4), -6)] # access everything EXCEPT columns 1 through 4 and column 6

mtcars["Duster 360" , "mpg"] # select the mpg (column) for only Duster 360 (row)

```

Select the horse power data for the Duster 360, Lincoln Continental, and Maserati Bora. Instead of manually viewing the matrix to determine which rows and column numbers you want to specify, use rownames() and colnames().

```{r exercise-1-7}
rownames(mtcars)
colnames(mtcars)
mtcars[c("Duster 360", "Lincoln Continental", "Maserati Bora"), "hp"]
```


Oftentimes we want to edit data frames to add calculated columns, delete unnecessary rows, subset to a particular view, etc.

You can create a column using the "$" notation to specify the new column name, and "<-" to assign some values to the new column. The syntax is as follows:

```{r exercise-1-8}
# Syntax example: data_frame$new_column <- values
```

Let's try this out! In the mtcars data frame, there is a column called "am". This column holds transmission information where 0 = automatic, and 1 = manual. But as of now, this isn't very clear without knowing that information.

Create a new column called "transmission" that assigns the value "automatic" where am = 0, and "manual" where am = 1.

You can use an ifelse statement to assign your values! Remember, ifelse() takes in three arguments: ifelse(test_condition, yes, no)

```{r exercise-1-9}
mtcars$transmission <- ifelse(mtcars$am == 0, "automatic", "manual")
```

Now that we have the "transmission" column, the "am" column is no longer particularly useful. Let's delete it.

You can easily delete a row/column by subsetting around it using df[row, column] notation. Simply choose all of the rows/columns you want to keep (ignoring the ones you want to delete), and assign the subset to either the original data frame variable (to permanently delete the rows/columns), or to a new variable storing an edited copy of the data frame. In general, it is best to create a copy that way you always have access to your original unedited data frame if needed.

The syntax is as follows:

```{r exercise-1-10}
# Syntax example: df_copy <- df[rows_to_keep, columns_to_keep]
```

Use the above syntax to save a copy of the mtcars data without the "am" column. Remember to use colnames() to find the column number of "am". Also recall that to select row/columns to drop (hence selecting everything else), you can use "-index #".

```{r exercise-1-11}
which(colnames(mtcars) == "am")
mtcars_copy <- mtcars[, -which(colnames(mtcars) == "am")]
```

View your new mtcars copy data frame to check that the "am" column was dropped.

```{r exercise-1-12}
colnames(mtcars_copy)
head(mtcars_copy)
stopifnot(!"am" %in% colnames(mtcars_copy))
```



###### (2) Query and retrieve the TCGA breast cancer clinical data 
Now that you've worked with a simpler example dataset, it is time to work with TCGA breast cancer clinical dataset!

Reuse the BCR Biotab clinical data downloaded for Materials Download Part 2. If a CSV from this notebook already exists, read it instead. Otherwise read the downloaded `clinical_patient_brca` tab-separated file; this is the patient table that the previous assignment selected from `GDCprepare(clin_query)` after removing its two metadata rows.

```{r clinical-query}
if (file.exists(clinical_csv)) {
  clinic <- read.csv(clinical_csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
} else {
  # The earlier assignment's query used data.format = "BCR Biotab" and then:
  # clinical.BCRtab.all <- GDCprepare(clin_query)
  # clinic <- clinical.BCRtab.all$clinical_patient_brca[-c(1, 2), ]
  # Reading the downloaded TSV directly avoids a new GDC API request.
  # TCGAbiolinks::GDCprepare(clin_query)$clinical_patient_brca reads this same TSV.
  clinic <- read.delim(patient_files[[1]], check.names = FALSE,
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE, quote = "", comment.char = "",
                       na.strings = c("", "NA", "[Not Available]", "[Not Applicable]"))
  if (!"bcr_patient_barcode" %in% names(clinic)) {
    stop("The downloaded file is not a BCR Biotab patient table: ",
         patient_files[[1]])
  }
  # The prior homework dropped the first two metadata rows; recognize patients
  # by barcode so the same result works if metadata row counts change.
  patient_barcode <- as.character(clinic$bcr_patient_barcode)
  patient_mask <- !is.na(patient_barcode) &
    grepl("^TCGA-[A-Za-z0-9]{2}-[A-Za-z0-9]{4}$", patient_barcode)
  clinic <- clinic[patient_mask, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(clinic)) stop("No TCGA patient rows were found in ", patient_files[[1]])
}

if ("bcr_patient_barcode" %in% names(clinic)) {
  names(clinic)[names(clinic) == "bcr_patient_barcode"] <- "Tumor_Sample_Barcode"
}
required_columns <- c("Tumor_Sample_Barcode", "age_at_diagnosis", "gender",
                      "vital_status", "last_contact_days_to", "death_days_to")
missing_columns <- setdiff(required_columns, names(clinic))
if (length(missing_columns)) {
  stop("The clinical table is missing the expected BCR Biotab columns: ",
       paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "),
       ". Check the Materials Download Part 2 clinical query.")
}

# BCR Biotab age_at_diagnosis is in years; the two follow-up fields are in days.
clinic$age_at_diagnosis <- as_num(clinic$age_at_diagnosis)
clinic$last_contact_days_to <- as_num(clinic$last_contact_days_to)
clinic$death_days_to <- as_num(clinic$death_days_to)
clinic$vital_status <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(trimws(as.character(clinic$vital_status))))
clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode <- as.character(clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode)
if (nrow(clinic) < 500L ||
    !all(c("TCGA-4H-AAAK", "TCGA-3C-AAAU") %in% clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode)) {
  stop("The clinical table does not appear to be the full TCGA-BRCA patient table ",
       "from the previous assignment.")
}
```

Save the clinical table as a CSV in `analysis_data` on CARC so later runs can read it directly:

```{r}
write.csv(clinic, clinical_csv, row.names = FALSE)
```

To read the csv back into your environment as a dataframe:

```{r}
clinic <- read.csv(clinical_csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
```


###### (3) Exploring the Data

View the structure of the data as well as the first few lines. What two commands should you use?
Answer the following questions based on the output of those commands: 
# 1. How many rows are there? How many columns?
# 2. What is the data type of $gender?
# 3. What is the age in years of the 5th patient (barcode: TCGA-4H-AAAK)?
# 4. How old was the 1st patient at their last follow up (barcode: TCGA-3C-AAAU)? HINT: you need to look at data from two columns to answer this

```{r exercise-3-1}
str(clinic)
head(clinic)
dim(clinic)
class(clinic$gender)

patient_5 <- clinic[clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode %in% "TCGA-4H-AAAK", , drop = FALSE]
patient_1 <- clinic[clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode %in% "TCGA-3C-AAAU", , drop = FALSE]
patient_5[, c("Tumor_Sample_Barcode", "age_at_diagnosis"), drop = FALSE]
patient_1[, c("Tumor_Sample_Barcode", "age_at_diagnosis",
              "last_contact_days_to"), drop = FALSE]

age_at_last_follow_up <- function(patient) {
  if (!nrow(patient)) return(NA_real_)
  age <- as_num(patient$age_at_diagnosis[1])
  follow_up <- as_num(patient$last_contact_days_to[1])
  if (!is.finite(age) || !is.finite(follow_up)) return(NA_real_)
  age + follow_up / 365.25
}
first_follow_up_age <- age_at_last_follow_up(patient_1)
``` 

1. **Rows and columns:** `r nrow(clinic)` rows and `r ncol(clinic)` columns.
2. **Type of `gender`:** `r paste(class(clinic$gender), collapse = ", ")`.
3. **TCGA-4H-AAAK's age at diagnosis:** `r age_text(as_num(patient_5$age_at_diagnosis))`.
4. **TCGA-3C-AAAU's approximate age at last follow-up:** `r age_text(first_follow_up_age)`.
   This adds follow-up days/365.25 to the recorded age at diagnosis.

###### (4) Plotting

Choose two variables and make a scatter plot (use the plot() function).

THINK: what types of variables can you use in a scatter plot (continuous, discrete, categorical). Look these up if you need help!

For an extra challenge, add a plot title, axes titles, and colors to your plot.

```{r exercise-4-1}
# Two numeric variables among deceased patients: age and days to death.
dead_plot <- clinic$vital_status %in% "Dead" &
  is.finite(as_num(clinic$age_at_diagnosis)) &
  is.finite(as_num(clinic$death_days_to))
plot(as_num(clinic$age_at_diagnosis[dead_plot]),
     as_num(clinic$death_days_to[dead_plot]) / 365.25,
     xlab = "Age at diagnosis (years)", ylab = "Time to death (years)",
     main = "TCGA-BRCA: age and time to death", pch = 16,
     col = grDevices::adjustcolor("steelblue4", alpha.f = 0.5))
```

Choose two new variables and make a box plot (use the boxplot() function).

THINK: what types of variables can you use in a box plot?

For an extra challenge, add a plot title, axes titles, and confidence intervals to your plot.

```{r exercise-4-2}
# Two different variables: gender and time to last contact among living patients.
alive_plot <- clinic$vital_status %in% "Alive" &
  is.finite(as_num(clinic$last_contact_days_to)) &
  !is.na(clinic$gender) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(clinic$gender)))
box_data <- data.frame(
  follow_up_years = as_num(clinic$last_contact_days_to[alive_plot]) / 365.25,
  gender = clinic$gender[alive_plot]
)
boxplot(follow_up_years ~ gender, data = box_data,
        xlab = "Gender", ylab = "Time to last contact (years)",
        main = "TCGA-BRCA: follow-up among living patients",
        col = "lightblue", notch = TRUE)
```


###### (5) Boolean Masking

As discussed in lecture, a boolean mask is a vector of True and False values that allow for fast and efficient indexing of large dataframes in R. Boolean masks work as an extremely helpful implementation of R's vectorization abilities. 

A significant portion of your coding work will be data cleaning and preparation using boolean masks. As such, it's important you are comfortable with making them.

1) Create a mask to remove all NA values from vital_status
```{r}
# Filled in example for you! 
vital_status_na_mask <- !is.na(clinic$vital_status)

```

2) Create a mask to select for male patients
```{r}
male_mask <- !is.na(clinic$gender) &
  tolower(trimws(as.character(clinic$gender))) == "male"
```

3) Create a mask for patients under 35 or over 60. The next item instead asks for under 30 or over 60, so both masks are computed below. 
```{r}
# The worksheet uses <35 here but <30 in the following item; retain both.
age_values <- as_num(clinic$age_at_diagnosis)
under35_over60_mask <- is.finite(age_values) & (age_values < 35 | age_values > 60)
under30_over60_mask <- is.finite(age_values) & (age_values < 30 | age_values > 60)
```

4) Using your under30_over60_mask, create a new dataframe called no_middle_clinic which contains all the clinical data for patients under the age of 30 or over 60 at diagnosis

```{r}
no_middle_clinic <- clinic[under30_over60_mask, , drop = FALSE]
head(no_middle_clinic)
```


###### (6) Kaplan-Meier Plotting

To create a KM plot in R, we first need some packages. If any are missing, run `install.packages(c("survival", "survminer", "ggplot2"))` in the CARC RStudio Console, restart R, then Knit again.

```{r}
# Packages were checked in the setup chunk, before the clinical analysis.

```

After installing packages as needed, we still need to load them into R to use them in our code.

```{r}
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(ggplot2)
```

A KM plot allows us to stratify survival by some clinical feature (or -omic feature!) of interest, therefore providing a simple and understandable plot for seeing how different aspects of a patient's health influence the severity of a disease. Because this requires grouping by a feature, KM plots always involve some categorical value plotted against survival percentage over time. As such, we need to first choose or otherwise create a categorical variable of interest.

For this example, let's create a KM plot to look at the relationship between breast cancer patient age and their rate of survival. 

# 1. Data Preprocessing

First, check if there are any NA values in age_at_diagnosis (Hint: use the is.na() function. If you don't remember how the function works, run ?is.na() in the console). Use Boolean indexing to remove the NA values.

```{r}
age_NA_mask <- is.finite(as_num(clinic$age_at_diagnosis))
cleaned_clinic <- clinic[age_NA_mask, , drop = FALSE]
cleaned_clinic$age_at_diagnosis <- as_num(cleaned_clinic$age_at_diagnosis)
```

Create a new column called "age_category" in cleaned_clinic that contains the value "Young" if age_at_diagnosis is <=35, "Middle" if >35 and < 50, and "Old" if >=50. (Hint: use ifelse())

Note: These age threshold are relatively arbitrary, and just the ages that we are using in this example. 

```{r}
cleaned_clinic$age_category <- factor(
  ifelse(cleaned_clinic$age_at_diagnosis <= 35, "Young",
         ifelse(cleaned_clinic$age_at_diagnosis < 50, "Middle", "Old")),
  levels = c("Young", "Middle", "Old")
)
```

KM plots also require a column for days of observed survival or follow-up after diagnosis. However, TCGA records survival over time two ways: last_contact_days_to for patients who are still alive, and death_days_to for patients who passed away. In the source data, a patient who is alive may have "[Not Applicable]" in the death-days field; numeric conversion treats that as missing. Therefore, we need to create a new column called survival_time that combines the information in these two columns so there are no NA values.

```{r}
cleaned_clinic$survival_time <- ifelse(
  cleaned_clinic$vital_status == "Dead",
  cleaned_clinic$death_days_to,
  cleaned_clinic$last_contact_days_to
)
```

If we check the data, we see that the values in survival_time are strings from the "" around each number. We need to convert the values to numeric in order to use them in the KM plot.
```{r}
cleaned_clinic$survival_time <- as_num(cleaned_clinic$survival_time)
```


Finally, we need to make a death event column that contains T if a patient has died, and F if the patient is alive. (Hint: cleaned_clinic$vital_status has "Alive" if a patient is alive and "Dead" if a patient passed.)
```{r}
cleaned_clinic$death_event <- cleaned_clinic$vital_status == "Dead"
valid_survival <- cleaned_clinic$vital_status %in% c("Alive", "Dead") &
  is.finite(cleaned_clinic$survival_time) & cleaned_clinic$survival_time >= 0
cleaned_clinic <- cleaned_clinic[valid_survival, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(nrow(cleaned_clinic) > 0,
          length(unique(cleaned_clinic$age_category)) >= 2)
table(cleaned_clinic$age_category, cleaned_clinic$death_event)
```

# 2. Create Survminer Objects

Run the following code block.
```{r}
survival_object <- Surv(time = cleaned_clinic$survival_time,
                        event = cleaned_clinic$death_event)

fit_object <- survfit(survival_object ~ age_category, data = cleaned_clinic)
```

# 3. Create the KM Plot

Run the following code block. The KM plot should appear in the plot tab on the right. Manually expand the tab if you get an error about the plot being too small. 
```{r}
survplot <- ggsurvplot(fit_object,
                       pval=TRUE,
                       ggtheme = theme(plot.margin = grid::unit(c(1,1,1,1), "cm")),
                       legend = 'right')

KM_plot <- survplot$plot + theme_bw() + theme(axis.title = element_text(size=20), 
                                              axis.text = element_text(size=16),
                                              legend.title = element_text(size=14),
                                              legend.text = element_text(size=12))

KM_plot
```

```{r km-answers}
# Compare curves at five years only where that group has observed follow-up.
estimate_at <- function(group, days) {
  group_times <- cleaned_clinic$survival_time[
    cleaned_clinic$age_category == group]
  if (!length(group_times) || max(group_times) < days) return(NA_real_)
  s <- summary(fit_object, times = days, extend = TRUE)
  index <- which(as.character(s$strata) == paste0("age_category=", group))
  if (length(index) != 1L) return(NA_real_)
  s$surv[index]
}
five_year <- setNames(
  vapply(levels(cleaned_clinic$age_category), estimate_at, numeric(1),
         days = 5 * 365.25),
  levels(cleaned_clinic$age_category)
)
old_15_year <- estimate_at("Old", 15 * 365.25)
log_rank <- survdiff(Surv(survival_time, death_event) ~ age_category,
                     data = cleaned_clinic)
km_p <- pchisq(log_rank$chisq, df = length(log_rank$n) - 1,
              lower.tail = FALSE)

best_answer <- if (all(is.finite(five_year))) {
  sprintf("%s (about %.1f%% at five years)", names(which.max(five_year)),
          100 * max(five_year))
} else "Cannot compare all three groups at five years with the available follow-up"
worst_answer <- if (all(is.finite(five_year))) {
  sprintf("%s (about %.1f%% at five years)", names(which.min(five_year)),
          100 * min(five_year))
} else "Cannot compare all three groups at five years with the available follow-up"
old_answer <- if (is.finite(old_15_year)) {
  sprintf("about %.1f%%", 100 * old_15_year)
} else {
  "not estimable: the Old group has insufficient follow-up at 15 years"
}
significance_answer <- if (km_p < 0.05) {
  "Yes at the 0.05 level; at least two age-group survival curves differ. This is an association, not proof that age causes the difference."
} else {
  "No at the 0.05 level; the data do not provide strong evidence of a difference among the age-group survival curves."
}
```

**Answers to the Kaplan–Meier questions**

1. **Y-axis:** Estimated probability of remaining alive (overall survival).
2. **X-axis:** Days since diagnosis (the units of `survival_time`).
3. **Greatest apparent survival:** `r best_answer`
4. **Worst apparent survival:** `r worst_answer`
5. **Old group's approximate 15-year survival:** `r old_answer`
6. **Log-rank p-value:** `r format.pval(km_p, digits = 3, eps = 1e-16)`.
   **Significant?** `r significance_answer`
